# Overview {-}

**Author:** Sean Westwood

I would like to make a cool visual triangle of these three points around a central "statistical concepts", but for now I have just written this useless sentence and three bullet points:

- functions 
- equations
- visualisations

The goal of this book is to build up statistical understanding from these three different angles. You may have already encountered some combination of these, but perhaps don't yet feel an intuition for how they all link together. We will peel back the confusing abstractions and jargon, and walk you through each side of the triangle step-by-step until the full picture clicks into place.

**Important:** you do not need to know anything more advanced than **adding and dividing** to get started with the first concept in this book! Everything beyond that will be built directly from what we walk through together. If all you have right now is a vague understanding of an "average", this is the resource for you. 

<div class="summary-box">
A statistical formula is like a blueprint: a set of instructions for turning inputs (e.g. some data) into an output (e.g. a standard deviation)

A statistical function is the machine you build from the blueprint. You give it the inputs, it carries out the instructions, and it gives you back the output.

A statistical visualisation is a picture that links the cold hard numbers to what they mean in the real world.
</div>

If this book does its job well, students should be able to:

- describe a function as **input -> process -> output**
- translate simple mathematical notation into R code
- build functions from scratch for various summary and test statistics from their equations
- intuit how common visual representations of statistics represent the underlying numbers
- understand how different tests and models relate to each other mathematically

## How To Use This Book

Start with [Getting Started](#getting-started), which sets up an RStudio project for your work. The rough outline is that you will have an R script to add your own custom-built functions to so that you can access them whenever you like. Each chapter has its own exercises to download and follow along to, to help you build and apply this personal toolkit of functions. 

The recommended route is then to work through the parts in order. If you would rather build intuitions about null hypothesis testing sooner, the companion book [Demystifying Null Hypothesis Testing](https://demystr.github.io/nhst/) only assumes knowledge taught in the one-sample t-test chapter, starting with Null Distributions and then p-values.

- **Part I: Basics and Summary Statistics.** What functions are, how to turn an equation into code, and the summary statistics everything else is built from: the mean, variance, standard deviation and standard error.
- **Part II: Inferential Tests.** We will build brick-by-brick every piece of each test statistic as your own R function, starting from the summary statistics in Part I, and check each one against the *pro* version that most people use with R.
- **Part III: The General Linear Model.** In the same way we can understand how a t-test relates to the mean and variance of a sample, we can understand how a general linear model framework can express the exact same ideas in a different way. This part aims to rebuild the tests from Part II under one model.

Non-parametric tests have their own book, [Demystifying Non-Parametric Tests](https://demystr.github.io/nonparametric/): when we have less strong beliefs about the shape and qualities of our data, we can employ similar techniques that look at the relative position of each data point in the dataset, rather than its actual value.
